content.p: On the morning of Saturday 3 November 1979, a column of cars carrying Ku Klux Klansmen and American Nazis drove into Morningside Homes, a public housing project in Greensboro, North Carolina, where about 150 people had gathered for an anti-Klan march. Local television crews were there to film the start of the demonstration. They recorded what followed. According to the University of North Carolina library timeline, the shooting lasted 88 seconds. Four people were dead at the scene and a fifth, Dr. Michael Nathan, died in hospital two days later.

Two criminal trials, one in state court and one in federal court, ended in acquittals for the men who fired, all of whom said they had acted in self-defense. A 1985 civil jury reached a different result for one of the victims. The case has since been argued over for more than four decades: over who started the violence, what Greensboro's police and two informants knew beforehand, and whether the word "massacre" fits.
content.h2: Two movements on a collision course
content.p: The UNC library guide places the killings in the late 1970s, when Klan recruiting was growing in North Carolina and Klansmen and neo-Nazis, groups that had rarely worked together, were beginning to ally. At the same time, activists in the Piedmont were organizing around wages, workplace health and race. Several medical workers linked to the Communist Workers Party took jobs in textile mills, partly to press for protection against byssinosis, the cotton-dust lung disease known as brown lung. In Greensboro they teamed up with Black organizers, among them Nelson Johnson and Sandi Smith, a nursing student who was leading a union drive at a Cone Mills plant.

NCpedia, the state's online encyclopedia, notes that clashes with the Klan had already occurred in 1979 at Winston-Salem in April and at China Grove in July. Neither involved gunfire. At China Grove, the UNC timeline says, Klansmen showing the film "Birth of a Nation" were forced to shelter inside a community center while demonstrators surrounded it. A leaflet campaign then raised the temperature. An open letter called the Klan "a bunch of two-bit cowards" and invited them to a "Death to the Klan" march and conference on 3 November. The Communist Workers Party announced the march on 4 October.

Rev. Nelson Johnson, speaking to the Associated Press in 2017, said that both the "Death to the Klan" billing and the group's decision to rename itself the Communist Workers Party had been mistakes. He said the event was meant to be about workers, mill wages and brown lung.

The UNC timeline sets out, day by day, how the Klan and Nazis prepared. Edward Dawson, a longtime Klansman, had been an FBI informant from 1970 to 1977 and was working with Greensboro police detective Jerry "Rooster" Cooper in 1979. On 20 October, the timeline says, he gave a "fiery speech" at a Klan rally in Lincoln County urging a confrontation with the Communist Workers Party. On 21 October he told Cooper that 250 Klansmen would come to Greensboro. On 31 October he reported to a police lieutenant, Paul Spoon, and obtained a copy of the march's parade permit. According to the timeline, the permit gave a meeting point that was not on the organizers' flyers.

The second informant, Bernard Butkovich, was an agent of the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms who had posed as a long-distance trucker to join the American Nazi Party's Winston-Salem unit. In later testimony, the timeline says, Nazis from that unit said Butkovich offered to improve their arsenal. History.com goes further and says he supplied some of the firearms used. Butkovich was present in September when Klan and Nazi leaders agreed to form a "United Racist Front", and on 1 November he and Dawson attended a Nazi planning meeting in Winston-Salem.

According to the timeline, at about 10 a.m. on the day, Dawson phoned Detective Cooper to say the Klan was armed and violence was imminent. At 10:25 he gave the order for the convoy to move, riding in the lead car. Around 11:13 a neo-Nazi named Jack Fowler arrived with weapons, including an automatic rifle, and was told to join the rear of the line.

The police side of the planning is also in the timeline. Because the Greensboro Police Department had long been hostile toward the Communist Workers Party, it chose a "low profile". After a sergeant doubted that six officers could handle the 80 to 85 Klansmen and Nazis Dawson had predicted, a tactical squad was added. NCpedia says only four officers were assigned to accompany the marchers, while the UNC timeline speaks of six. Because the march was due to start at noon, the officers were not present when the Klan cars arrived early. History.com describes the tactical squad as "suspiciously absent" when the Klan and Nazis arrived. The state's historical marker says police arrived after the shooting was over.

Around 11:20 a.m., the timeline says, the caravan reached the corner of Everitt Street and Carver Drive. The Klansmen and Nazis got out and began unloading weapons from the last car. NCpedia gives the time of the first shot as 11:23.

The dead were Sandra Neely Smith, Cesar Cauce, James Waller and William Evan Sampson, killed at the scene, and Dr. Michael Nathan. INDY Week describes two of them, Nathan and Waller, as doctors, and the others as labor activists. The count of wounded varies by source: WUNC and the state marker say ten, the UNC timeline says eleven.

What happened in the first seconds is disputed. History.com says that videotape shows demonstrators starting the violence by kicking and striking the Klan and Nazi cars, and that the Communist Workers Party members, who carried concealed weapons, returned fire after the Klansmen and Nazis began shooting. The Greensboro Truth and Reconciliation Commission, as quoted by NPR, said party members did not seek or deserve to be killed. But it said they underestimated the danger of taunting the Klan with provocative language and of beating on caravan cars with sticks, and that a few members also fired guns once the shooting had begun. Johnson told the AP that a Nazi stabbed him in the arm as he defended himself.

Afterwards Greensboro's own words for the day split along the same line. NCpedia notes that the organizers and their allies called it a "massacre", while many residents called it a "shootout", which put blame on both sides.

In 1980, six Klan and Nazi members stood trial on murder and rioting charges, according to History.com. Evidence emerged during the trial that police, and possibly federal agencies, had known violence was likely. The jury, which NCpedia describes as all white, acquitted the defendants. INDY Week dates the verdicts to about a year after the attack and notes that the defendants had been filmed. The defendants said they fired in self-defense.

The FBI, under the code name GREENKIL, then conducted an investigation, and in 1983, NCpedia says, a federal grand jury indicted nine Klan and Nazi suspects on charges of conspiring to violate the marchers' civil rights. At the 1984 federal trial, a jury also found them not guilty. WUNC and the state marker both report that the defendants claimed self-defense in each case, and WUNC adds that both juries were all white.

The survivors then took a civil action. NCpedia says they sued the Klan, the Nazi party, the Greensboro Police Department, the FBI and the ATF for $48 million, alleging negligence by named officers because an informant had advance knowledge of the Klan's and Nazis' plans to arm themselves and confront the marchers. In 1985, according to History.com, a North Carolina jury held two Greensboro police officers, five Klan and Nazi defendants and Edward Dawson responsible for the wrongful death of a single demonstrator, with damages of nearly $400,000. The UNC timeline names the two officers as Detective Cooper and Lieutenant Spoon, and names the victim as Michael Nathan. History.com adds that the jury found no conspiracy among the Klan, local police and the federal government. NCpedia observes that only 7 of the 65 individuals sued were found liable.

The city paid $351,000 to Nathan's family, the state marker says. NC WARN, the publisher of a statement by the Beloved Community Center, adds that the city denied wrongdoing at the time, that the Klan and Nazis paid nothing, and that this was the first time in US history that Klansmen, Nazis and police officers had been found jointly liable for a wrongful death. That claim of a first is the group's own and is not confirmed by the other pages.
content.h2: The truth commission and the apology
content.p: Two decades after the killings, a group of local residents and survivors began campaigning for a community truth process. JusticeInfo.net dates the commission to 1999 and says it began taking testimony in 2000, while the Guilfordian dates the effort to 2004. Both call it the first such process in the United States. It had seven commissioners, held three public hearings and heard from former Klan members, police officers, survivors and neighbors. The city council declined to endorse it, NPR reported, and the then mayor, Keith Holliday, had said it was being steered by former Communist Workers Party members.

Its report, more than 500 pages long, was released on 25 May 2006. Commissioner Pat Clark told listeners that the main contributor to the loss of life was the absence of police, and that nearly all commissioners believed the absence was in some measure intentional. The report described a "stunning lack of curiosity and planning for the safety of the event". Marty Nathan, widow of Michael Nathan, said it drew the conclusion that police were complicit with the Klan. City police officials were unavailable for comment, NPR said, and the Guilfordian reported in 2010 that the council had voted the previous summer to continue to ignore and reject its findings.

Recognition came slowly. In 2015 the state erected a highway marker headed "Greensboro Massacre", a word the commission's report had avoided, the AP noted. The state marker text records that the commission had also recommended a public monument at the site and that, so far, none had been built. The victims are buried in Maplewood Cemetery in Greensboro.

On 6 October 2020 the city council voted 7 to 2 to apologize for the police department's role. WUNC reported that the resolution acknowledged police knew of the planned attack. It also set up annual scholarships of $1,979 for five students at James B. Dudley High School, one for each victim. Councilwoman Nancy Hoffman, who voted against, said she saw nothing in the contemporaneous reporting that convinced her of collusion or of malicious action or inaction by the police. Councilwoman Marikay Abuzuaiter also voted no. Mayor Nancy Vaughan said the apology did not criticize the current police department. Marty Nathan said afterwards that further steps lay ahead.
